procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 13.10.1982 in Writ Petition No. 501-A of 1982 (for Civil Appeal No. 4041 of 1982) and Judgement and Order dated 1.12.1982 in W.P. No. 1976 of 1982 (for Civil Appeal No. 4363 of 1985)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court declined to interfere with the orders challenged in petitions filed under Article 226 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court because they contended that the impugned orders of dismissal suffered from a total non-application of mind.

directions: The Inspector-General of Police is directed to entertain applications for revision by the Appellants by relaxing the period of limitation and hearing such applications on the merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the dismissal order was invalid because the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry did not accompany the order, but were served separately.

facts: The dismissal order served on each appellant already contained the reasons why it was not reasonably practicable to hold an inquiry.
A separate document, also titled "reasons", was served later.
This separate document merely "amplified and elaborated" on the reasons that were already stated in the original dismissal order.
law: The recording of reasons for dispensing with an inquiry is a mandatory condition precedent for a valid dismissal under clause (b) of the second proviso to Article 311(2) of the Constitution.
If reasons are not recorded in writing, the dismissal order is void and unconstitutional.
While it is not strictly necessary for the reasons to be in the final order, it is advisable to include them to avoid allegations that they were fabricated later.
application: The Court examined the dismissal order and found that it did, in fact, set out the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry.
The Court determined that since the reasons were included in the order itself, the core legal requirement was met.
The separately served document was not a late justification but simply an elaboration of the reasons already provided with the order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and held that the dismissal was valid. It found there was "no substance in the contention that the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry did not accompany the order" because the dismissal order itself contained the necessary reasons.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the dismissal order was invalid because the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry did not accompany the order, but were served separately.
appellant_arguments: The impugned orders of dismissal were invalid because they suffered from a total non-application of mind.
The dismissal order was invalid because the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry were not included with the order itself, but were served separately.
respondent_arguments: In the instant case, the impugned orders of dismissal served on each of the appellants itself sets out the reasons why it was not reasonably practicable to hold an inquiry.
The 'reasons' served separately merely amplified and elaborated what had been stated in the impugned order.
There is no substance in the contention that the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry did not accompany the order.

cases.case_name: Satyavir Singh and Ors. etc. v. Union of India & Ors.
cases.principle: The Court followed this precedent in its overall application and interpretation of Article 311(2) of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: Union of India & Anr. v. Tulsiram Patel & Ors.
cases.principle: The validity of using cyclostyled orders of dismissal is not a universal rule and depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a situation where the acts alleged were of a large group acting collectively with the common object of coercing the authority, and it is not possible to particularize the acts of each individual member of the group, the general rule requiring particularization may not apply.
obiter: Whether a rule is universal depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The dismissal order was not invalid because, contrary to the appellant's contention, the order itself contained the reasons for dispensing with the inquiry. The separate document served later merely amplified and elaborated upon the reasons that were already stated in the impugned order, thus satisfying the legal requirement.
legal_tests_applied: The recording of reasons for dispensing with an inquiry is a condition precedent to the applicability of cl. (b) of the second proviso to Art. 311(2) of the Constitution; and, if such reasons are not recorded in writing, the order dispensing with the inquiry and the order of penalty following thereupon would both be void and unconstitutional.

While it is not strictly necessary that the reasons find a place in the final order imposing the penalty, it is advisable to record them in the final order to avoid an allegation that the reasons were fabricated subsequently.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument failed because its factual premise was incorrect; the impugned order of dismissal itself set out the reasons why it was not reasonably practicable to hold the inquiry.

The document containing "reasons" that was served separately was found to be merely an amplification and elaboration of what had already been stated in the dismissal order, not the sole or initial recording of those reasons.
why_respondent_won: The dismissal order was valid because it explicitly stated that due to the collective acts of insubordination, indiscipline, and rioting, any attempt to hold a departmental inquiry would be frustrated by the collective action of the concerned persons, making it not reasonably practicable.
policy_considerations: To serve the ends of justice, even while upholding the dismissal order's validity, the Court directed the Inspector-General of Police to entertain applications for revision from the appellants by relaxing the period of limitation and hearing the applications on their merits.
